issues.description: Normalization only handles ClassName; IDs, attributes, tags, pseudos with escapes are silently ignored
issues.detail: The bug is about CSS escape-sequence equivalence — a value-level fact about selectors. That fact applies equally to `#u-m\+` vs `#u-m\00002b`, to `[data-x=\+]`, to tag selectors with escapes, and to pseudo-class arguments. Restricting `normalizeNodeEscaping` to `parser.isClassName(node)` complects the general concern (escape normalization is a property of identifier values) with one incidental node type. The same class of false negative still exists for every other escapable identifier.

issues.description: `node.value = node.value` complects intent with a language quirk; the operation is invisible without the comment
issues.detail: The code relies on the side effect that postcss-selector-parser's setter re-escapes through a getter that unescapes. The operation `node.value = node.value` reads as a no-op everywhere except inside this one library's accessor pair. The intent — `normalizeEscaping(node.value)` — is a value transformation on a string. Pulling the unescape/re-escape into a named pure function (taking and returning a string) would separate the value transform from the mutation, make it testable in isolation, and stop depending on an implementation detail of a third-party setter that may change. As written it is easy (short) but not simple (one concept, decomposable).

issues.description: `raws.value` early-return is a performance optimization that couples to undocumented internal state
issues.detail: The guard `if (!node.raws?.value) return;` is reaching past the typed API into `raws` (acknowledged by the `@ts-expect-error`) to skip the self-assign when no escaping was present. That is incidental complexity introduced for a micro-optimization, and it ties this function to a private shape of the parser. If the normalization is expressed as a pure string function, the no-op case is trivially cheap and this guard disappears.

issues.description: Tests cover the happy path for ClassName only; no test pins the scope of what is normalized
issues.detail: Two reject cases plus two pass cases all exercise `.u-m\+`-style class selectors. There is no test for `#id\+`, attribute selectors with escapes, escaped tag names, or escaped pseudo arguments — so the implicit scope of the fix is undocumented. Either add a passing test that asserts non-class escapes are intentionally out of scope, or add reject tests that prove they are handled. Right now the test suite does not tell a future reader which fact about the world this code represents.

review.summary: The fix works for the reported case but is EASY-NOT-SIMPLE. It encodes "normalize CSS escaping" as a self-assignment that piggybacks on postcss-selector-parser's getter/setter pair, and only for `ClassName` nodes. The underlying fact — two selectors with different escape sequences denote the same identifier — applies to IDs, attributes, tag names, and pseudo arguments too; restricting to ClassName is incidental and leaves the same bug class open elsewhere. The hammock question that should have come first: "what is the canonical form of a selector value, as a pure value transformation?" A small `normalizeEscaping(string) -> string` helper applied wherever an identifier appears would be simple; `node.value = node.value` guarded by a private `raws` poke is COMPLECTED with a library implementation detail.
